newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate moving toward vote on tax bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate moving toward vote on tax bill.

text.p: The Senate was moving Friday toward passage of legislation to give Americans the biggest tax cut in 16 years, a day after the House approved its tax bill.

House and Senate negotiators in coming weeks will try to work out differences in the two bills so a final package can be sent to the president. The legislation would implement the tax portion of last month's pact between congressional leaders and the White House to balance the budget over five years.

The White House reiterated Friday both bills were unacceptable to President Clinton in their present form. "The president wants a tax cut. He wants a targeted tax cut, and the House and Senate measures don't quite muster up at this point," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Clinton, however, said he was "quite optimistic" the White House and Congress would reach agreement on the details. "We should expect a little of this skirmishing. We're going to offer our thoughts on Monday," Clinton said.
Senate debate on the five-year $77 billion net tax cut bill was in the third day with most amendments failing to pass. A final vote on the bill was expected later Friday.
One proposal that was approved would gradually increase the amount of tax deduction self-employed individuals could take for health insurance, eventually reaching 100 percent.

The Senate defeated a proposal from Sen. Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, to raise the cigarette tax by 23 cents per pack to pay for children's health programmes. That would have been in addition to the 20-cent-per-pack tobacco tax increase already in the Senate bill.
Senate Budget Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, was angered by the administration's support of Kennedy's proposal, saying it violated the budget agreement.
The Senate bill was drafted with more bipartisan support than the House tax cut, and Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota has said he planned to vote for it.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, the senior Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee that produced the tax bill, said prospects were "not large" for any major changes to the legislation at this point.

The Senate bill would provide a $500 tax credit for each child under age 17 and require that the credit be deposited in a type of Individual Retirement Account for education for children aged 13 to 16.
Also included were tax relief for college education costs and expanded Individual Retirement Accounts.

Married couples would be allowed to exclude from taxation up to $500,000 of gain made from selling a home. The bill would cut the capital gains tax on profits made on investments such as stocks to 20 percent from the maximum 28 percent rate for individuals.

The bill would raise the threshold where the estate tax is imposed to $1 million in 2006 from $600,000 now, and immediately exclude $1 million from tax when a family-owned business comprised more than 50 percent of the estate.

Higher taxes and elimination of certain tax breaks would raise $66 billion in revenues over five years. Those included extension of airline ticket taxes and higher passenger fees, a 20-cent-per-pack increase in the cigarette tax, and a gradual reduction in the ethanol subsidy starting in 2001.
